classification.difficultyReason: Apply the definition to familiar expressions, including negative and fractional powers, irrational coefficients and constants.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 supplies the definition and constant case; Example 1 on pages 3–4 rejects a negative index and accepts real fractional coefficients and constants. Example 2 on page 4 demonstrates expansion before describing a polynomial.
questions.methodNote: Apply the definition: a polynomial has real coefficients and whole-number powers of its variable. Expand a squared binomial when necessary; constants are degree-zero polynomials.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the definition to familiar expressions, including negative and fractional powers, irrational coefficients and constants.

classification.difficultyReason: Reorder polynomial terms and identify three defining features, including missing constant terms and a constant polynomial.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–i directly assesses the polynomial features defined on page 2 and summarised on page 3. Example 1 on pages 3–4 models rearrangement and the constant-polynomial case; Example 2 on page 4 models reporting the requested three features.
questions.methodNote: Arrange terms in descending powers, then identify the highest exponent, its coefficient and the term independent of x. A missing constant term is zero; a non-zero constant polynomial has degree zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reorder polynomial terms and identify three defining features, including missing constant terms and a constant polynomial.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the leading coefficient, rearranging or simplifying expressions where necessary, and compare it with 1.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess the monic definition on pages 2–3 and Example 1, continued on page 4. Parts c and e require descending-order identification; part d uses the constant-polynomial convention; part f first simplifies division by 6.
questions.methodNote: Identify the term with highest index after arranging or simplifying the polynomial. A polynomial is monic exactly when its leading coefficient is 1; a non-zero constant is a polynomial of degree 0.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the leading coefficient, rearranging or simplifying expressions where necessary, and compare it with 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of numerical and simple algebraic arguments, including negative arguments and a cubic power.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f assess numerical polynomial evaluation; parts g–i extend the same substitution method to algebraic arguments, making evaluation at an algebraic argument the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Replace every occurrence of x by the argument, retaining brackets for negative or algebraic arguments; evaluate powers before combining terms. Page 3 demonstrates numerical and algebraic substitution, and Example 3 on page 4 demonstrates positive, zero, negative and doubled algebraic arguments.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of numerical and simple algebraic arguments, including negative arguments and a cubic power.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct numerical substitution into four polynomials, retaining signs when evaluating negative arguments.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess numerical evaluation of a named polynomial, so polynomial-notation-evaluate is the closest existing skill.
questions.methodNote: Use function notation, substitute each numerical argument for every occurrence of x, evaluate powers before products, then combine signed terms. Parentheses preserve negative arguments. Page 3 demonstrates numerical substitution; Example 3 on page 4 demonstrates positive, negative and zero arguments.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct numerical substitution into four polynomials, retaining signs when evaluating negative arguments.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute given arguments to find unknown coefficients; part c requires forming and solving two simultaneous linear equations.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b directly apply page 4 Example 4. Part c applies the same substitution twice, then uses the elimination and substitution method explicitly demonstrated on page 16; no factor theorem is needed because both function values are already supplied.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 introduces polynomial evaluation by substitution. Page 4 Example 4 substitutes a supplied argument and solves the resulting linear equation for a coefficient. Page 16 Example 12 explicitly demonstrates forming two coefficient equations, eliminating an unknown and substituting back.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute given arguments to find unknown coefficients; part c requires forming and solving two simultaneous linear equations.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct polynomials from coefficient constraints and determine an unknown coefficient by substitution.

questions.mappingNote: Part a fixes the leading and constant coefficients before substitution; part b selects a valid quartic form and determines its linear coefficient; part c assigns one common coefficient to all five terms and evaluates at -1. These directly combine polynomial descriptions and evaluation.
questions.methodNote: Use degree, leading coefficient, monic and constant-term definitions from page 2; substitute into polynomial notation as demonstrated on pages 3–4; solve a linear coefficient equation as in Example 4 on page 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct polynomials from coefficient constraints and determine an unknown coefficient by substitution.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply polynomial addition and subtraction, distributing a negative sign and collecting like terms.

questions.mappingNote: Every part asks for a sum and difference of explicitly given polynomials, directly matching Example 5's addition and subtraction method. The supplied reuse candidates have different givens and tasks, so none is source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 substitutes polynomial expressions in brackets, expands subtraction or numerical multipliers, and collects like terms in descending powers. The page 7 summary confirms the usual rules of algebra.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply polynomial addition and subtraction, distributing a negative sign and collecting like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand products of polynomials and collect like terms, including cancellation.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses polynomial multiplication.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 distributes each term over the second polynomial, expands and collects like terms in descending powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand products of polynomials and collect like terms, including cancellation.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalise the degree and constant-term rules from several polynomial products.

questions.mappingNote: The question generalises degree and constant-term behaviour from question 3.
questions.methodNote: Use the term-by-term multiplication and collection of like terms demonstrated in Example 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalise the degree and constant-term rules from several polynomial products.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalise three properties of polynomial squares, including both possible leading coefficients for a monic square.

questions.mappingNote: Generalises question 5's products to degree, constant term and monicity.
questions.methodNote: Use term-by-term multiplication to identify leading and constant terms in a square.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalise three properties of polynomial squares, including both possible leading coefficients for a monic square.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute three polynomial expressions, distribute signed terms and collect like terms.

questions.mappingNote: The expression resembles a division identity but the assessed task is expansion and simplification.
questions.methodNote: Combine Example 6's distribution with Example 5's addition and collection of like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute three polynomial expressions, distribute signed terms and collect like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Carry out whole-number division by two-digit divisors and express each result using its quotient and remainder.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 directly assesses this whole-number prerequisite. Part a can be calculated mentally; parts b and c use the demonstrated long-division method. Polynomial teaching on page 10 supplies topic context but is not required to solve these numerical divisions.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 demonstrates whole-number long division, successive subtraction and bringing down digits, then writes the dividend as divisor times quotient plus remainder. The remainder is less than the divisor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Carry out whole-number division by two-digit divisors and express each result using its quotient and remainder.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply successive leading-term division, including missing powers and a non-monic linear divisor, and express each result as an identity.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts use the leading-term division algorithm demonstrated on page 10 and in Example 7 on page 11. Parts c, d and e require missing-power placeholders; part e also requires division by the leading coefficient 2. The formal statement on page 12 supplies the requested identity and stopping condition.
questions.methodNote: Polynomial long division repeatedly divides the current leading term by the divisor's leading term, multiplies, subtracts and continues. Missing powers retain their columns through zero coefficients. Finish with P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R(x), with zero remainder or remainder degree smaller than the divisor's degree.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply successive leading-term division, including missing powers and a non-monic linear divisor, and express each result as an identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply successive leading-term division with quadratic divisors and identify linear remainders.

questions.mappingNote: Example 7 on PDF page 11 demonstrates division by a quadratic divisor and a linear remainder, directly matching both parts. Pages 9–10 introduce the division identity and repeated subtraction; page 12 states the remainder-degree condition.
questions.methodNote: Divide leading terms successively, multiply the divisor by each quotient term and subtract, retaining columns for missing powers. Stop when the remainder has degree below the divisor's degree.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply successive leading-term division with quadratic divisors and identify linear remainders.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply successive leading-term division with quadratic and cubic divisors and express each result as a division identity.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 Example 7 directly models division by a quadratic divisor; pages 10 and 12 establish the same algorithm and identity for polynomial divisors generally. Parts a and b require two quotient terms; c and d require three. Part d applies the same process to a cubic divisor.
questions.methodNote: Divide successive leading terms, multiply the divisor by each quotient term, subtract and repeat. Retain columns for missing powers. Stop when the remainder has smaller degree than the divisor, then write the division identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply successive leading-term division with quadratic and cubic divisors and express each result as a division identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the degree restriction on a non-zero remainder and the degree relationship in the division identity.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c apply the remainder-degree restriction stated on pages 10 and 12 and illustrated by the quadratic divisor in Example 7 on page 11. Part d applies the leading-term division method on page 10 to degrees 6 and 2. The offered reuse candidate matches only part c, so the complete four-part source question is authored normally.
questions.methodNote: Use the division identity P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R(x), with a zero remainder or a remainder of degree less than the divisor. Leading-term division determines the quotient's degree.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the degree restriction on a non-zero remainder and the degree relationship in the division identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Use polynomial long division to establish a zero remainder, then factorise the quotient and divisor completely.

questions.mappingNote: Example 8 on page 12 explicitly links long division with complete factorisation. Pages 10–11 demonstrate division by linear and quadratic divisors, covering the two assigned parts.
questions.methodNote: Divide leading terms, multiply the divisor by each quotient term and subtract, retaining successive powers in aligned columns. A zero remainder establishes divisibility; then factorise the quotient and divisor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use polynomial long division to establish a zero remainder, then factorise the quotient and divisor completely.

classification.difficultyReason: Perform polynomial long division and use the resulting remainder to determine coefficients giving exact divisibility.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the linear-divisor algorithm on page 10. Part b uses quadratic-divisor long division as in Example 7 on page 11. Each hence task adjusts the preceding division identity and sets its remainder to zero, using the divisibility statement on page 12.
questions.methodNote: Divide successive leading terms, multiply the divisor by each quotient term and subtract; stop when the remainder has smaller degree than the divisor. Exact divisibility requires zero remainder.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Perform polynomial long division and use the resulting remainder to determine coefficients giving exact divisibility.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate each polynomial at the zero of its linear divisor and use the remainder to decide whether the divisor is a factor.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly combine Example 10's remainder calculations with the factor criterion stated and demonstrated on page 16.
questions.methodNote: Use the remainder theorem to evaluate P at the zero of D, then apply the factor theorem: D is a factor exactly when that remainder is zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate each polynomial at the zero of its linear divisor and use the remainder to decide whether the divisor is a factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the polynomial at each linear divisor's zero and use the remainder to determine whether the divisor is a factor.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 uses the same direct substitution procedure as Examples 9 and 10, followed by the factor decision demonstrated and stated on page 16. All four divisors and the shared polynomial differ from the supplied reuse candidate, so ordinary authoring is required.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate P(alpha) for division by x-alpha. Rewrite x+alpha with a negative substitution as in Example 10. Apply the factor theorem: a zero remainder identifies a factor; a nonzero remainder excludes it.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate the polynomial at each linear divisor's zero and use the remainder to determine whether the divisor is a factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate each polynomial at negative one, handling odd and even powers, and use the zero-remainder criterion to identify factors.

questions.mappingNote: Every part has divisor x+1, so substitute x=-1. Page 15 Example 10 demonstrates negative substitutions and factor conclusions; page 16 explicitly states and demonstrates both factor-theorem outcomes. The high exponents in part f require only odd/even powers of -1.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate P at the zero of the monic linear divisor to obtain the remainder. Apply the factor theorem: zero remainder means the divisor is a factor; a nonzero remainder means it is not.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate each polynomial at negative one, handling odd and even powers, and use the zero-remainder criterion to identify factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the listed candidate factors to substitution values and apply the taught zero test systematically; the additional evaluations add repetition rather than a new reasoning decision.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts require systematic factor-theorem checks rather than polynomial division or factorisation by inspection. The six substitutions preserve the source candidate-factor order.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate P(alpha) at the zero of each linear divisor. A zero evaluation establishes a factor; a nonzero evaluation rules it out, as demonstrated on page 16.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert the listed candidate factors to substitution values and apply the taught zero test systematically; the additional evaluations add repetition rather than a new reasoning decision.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a stated linear factor into a zero remainder and solve a linear equation for an unknown coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses P(1)=0 and part b uses P(-2)=0. Each requires one linear coefficient equation, directly combining the coefficient method in Example 11 with the factor theorem on page 16. The offered reuse candidate has different polynomials and response requirements and is not source-identical.
questions.methodNote: The remainder theorem identifies the remainder as P(alpha); the factor theorem sets this equal to zero for a stated factor x-alpha. Example 11 solves for one unknown coefficient, and Example 12 explicitly applies zero-value conditions to stated factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a stated linear factor into a zero remainder and solve a linear equation for an unknown coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate each stated remainder into an evaluation equation and solve for one unknown coefficient, including a negative substitution.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess finding an unknown coefficient from a remainder. The supplied reuse candidate has different polynomials and response requirements, so it is not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: For division by x−α, the remainder equals P(α). Equate that evaluation to the stated remainder and solve for the unknown coefficient, as in Example 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate each stated remainder into an evaluation equation and solve for one unknown coefficient, including a negative substitution.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate remainder and divisibility conditions into simultaneous linear equations for two or three unknown coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All three vertically arranged parts belong to printed question 7. There is no shared verbal mathematical instruction; each part retains its complete givens.
questions.methodNote: Use the remainder or factor theorem to construct linear equations, then solve by elimination and substitution as demonstrated in Example 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate remainder and divisibility conditions into simultaneous linear equations for two or three unknown coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a monic quadratic from its factors and verify both zeros after expansion.

questions.methodNote: Write the product of the given factors, expand, then substitute each proposed zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a monic quadratic from its factors and verify both zeros after expansion.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a monic quartic directly from four given linear factors.

questions.methodNote: A monic polynomial is the product of its supplied monic factors without an additional multiplier.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a monic quartic directly from four given linear factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Verify a zero, carry out polynomial division and factor the resulting quadratic.

questions.methodNote: Substitute to verify a zero, divide by its linear factor using long division, then factor the quadratic quotient.

classification.difficultyReason: Select integer zeros and factor cubic polynomials, including repeated factors.

questions.mappingNote: Each cubic directly assesses the procedure demonstrated before Exercise 17E and in Example 13.
questions.methodNote: Test signed factors of the constant term, identify a zero, use long division and factor the quadratic quotient; retain repeated factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select integer zeros and factor cubic polynomials, including repeated factors.

questions.methodNote: Repeat zero testing and long division until the remaining quadratic can be factored; check repeated factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select integer root candidates, test and divide successively, then factor the quadratic quotient; repeated factors use the explicitly taught procedure.

questions.methodNote: Take out the common numerical factor or power of x first, then test zeros, divide and factor the quotient as in Example 14.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied common-factor instruction, then select integer roots and repeat division; part d requires recognising and retaining repeated factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Select integer roots, remove common factors where present, and repeatedly divide to leave one quadratic factor.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess factor-theorem factorisation; part c first removes a common power of x. The degree-five expression in c reduces to a cubic before applying the selected skill.
questions.methodNote: Remove common factors, test integer factors of the constant term using the factor theorem, and use long division repeatedly. Factorisations in this section use integer coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select integer roots, remove common factors where present, and repeatedly divide to leave one quadratic factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a general algebraic divisibility proof using an integer root and integer coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: This proof justifies the integer-root candidates used in the factor-theorem method on pages 18 and 20; factor-theorem is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the integer root, rearrange to isolate the constant term, and extract the common integer factor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a general algebraic divisibility proof using an integer root and integer coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the zero-product property to supplied linear factors, including repeated factors.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts solve supplied products using their linear factors; factor-theorem is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Examples 15–16 set each factor equal to zero; page 22 explains repeated roots. Solutions are real, as in Examples 17–18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the zero-product property to supplied linear factors, including repeated factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve linear and quadratic factors, retaining exact surds and rejecting quadratics without real roots.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b directly require the quadratic formula; c–d combine supplied factors with real-root decisions.
questions.methodNote: Use the zero-product property, then Example 18's quadratic formula for surd roots and Example 17's positivity or discriminant test for no real roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve linear and quadratic factors, retaining exact surds and rejecting quadratics without real roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Find integer roots, divide out linear factors and factor the remaining polynomial, including a quintic with a common square factor.

questions.mappingNote: The instruction explicitly requires the factor theorem. Part c first reduces its quintic to a cubic, fitting the same taught method.
questions.methodNote: Pages 18–20 test integer factors of the constant term, use polynomial long division and factor the quotient. Examples 15–16 apply the resulting factorisation to an equation; common powers of x are removed first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find integer roots, divide out linear factors and factor the remaining polynomial, including a quintic with a common square factor.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires finding a factorisation before solving. The quintics reduce by common or linear factors; factor-theorem remains the closest available skill despite the catalogue's degree wording.
questions.methodNote: Use integer-root trials and long division from pages 18–20, retaining repeated factors. Example 17 rejects a positive quadratic; Examples 17–18 solve the remaining factors over the reals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose integer root trials and repeat polynomial division, checking repeated factors and rejecting a positive quadratic; these are linked procedures explicitly taught in the preceding examples.

questions.mappingNote: Factor-theorem reductions are central in all four parts; quadratic formula and discriminant reasoning complete the real solution sets.
questions.methodNote: Apply the factor theorem and long division, then Example 18's quadratic formula or Example 17's positivity/discriminant test. Remove a common power of x first as in Examples 14 and 16.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose integer roots and repeatedly apply the factor theorem and long division, then use the quadratic formula or exclude non-real roots; these are routine linked procedures explicitly taught in the preceding examples.

classification.difficultyReason: Find zeros, determine signs between successive zeros and combine intercepts with end behaviour to sketch quadratic and cubic curves.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses graphing a polynomial already in factored form; all roots are simple. Pages 26–27 provide repeated-root contrast but are not needed to solve these parts.
questions.methodNote: Page 24 introduces zeros, y-intercepts, test points and sign diagrams. Example 19 on page 25 combines these with leading-term behaviour to sketch a polynomial with simple roots. The solutions follow that sequence without calculus.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find zeros, determine signs between successive zeros and combine intercepts with end behaviour to sketch quadratic and cubic curves.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify a repeated zero and use odd or even multiplicity to construct sign diagrams and translated power-curve sketches.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly compare the effects of multiplicities 2, 3 and 4 at the same zero, so polynomial-roots-multiplicity is the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Find zeros from the factors, determine interval signs, find the y-intercept, and sketch. Pages 25–26 explain flat crossings for odd repeated powers. Example 20 and the summary on page 27 explain touching for even powers and horizontal translation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify a repeated zero and use odd or even multiplicity to construct sign diagrams and translated power-curve sketches.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch three translated power curves, distinguishing touching from flat crossing at a repeated zero.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess translated power curves and repeated-root behaviour; polynomial-roots-multiplicity is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 26 sketches translated cubic powers using the zero, y-intercept and flat crossing. Page 27 Example 20 translates quartic powers and distinguishes even-multiplicity touching from odd-multiplicity crossing.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch three translated power curves, distinguishing touching from flat crossing at a repeated zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine three simple zeros, the vertical intercept and interval signs to sketch a cubic and identify where it lies above or below the horizontal axis.

questions.mappingNote: Sketching the factored cubic and interpreting its signs directly assess graph-polynomials-factored.
questions.methodNote: Page 24 teaches finding zeros and the vertical intercept, testing interval signs and drawing a smooth curve with the appropriate end behaviour. Example 19 on page 25 applies this sequence. Pages 26–27 distinguish repeated-root behaviour; this question has only simple roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine three simple zeros, the vertical intercept and interval signs to sketch a cubic and identify where it lies above or below the horizontal axis.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete difference-of-squares factorisations, identify zeros and combine signs and intercepts to sketch cubic and quartic curves.
